title: Structural transition in social networks: The role of homophily
publisher: arXiv (Murase, Jo, Török, Kertész, Kaski); Scientific Reports version

key_points.claim: Extends the weighted social network (WSN) model with F features per node, each with q values, to model homophily in tie formation. Agents' traits are fixed. This is a network-formation model in the spirit of Axelrod's.
key_points.evidence_quote: we assign a vector of F components to each node i, corresponding to F different features of the node

key_points.claim: Tie formation uses three mechanisms: global attachment (focal closure), local attachment (triadic closure) with weight reinforcement, and link deletion. Under homophily, links form only between nodes sharing the chosen feature's trait.
key_points.evidence_quote: it can make links only to the nodes sharing the same trait for the feature f

key_points.claim: Phase transition at Fc: for F<Fc the network is segregated into ~q^F homogeneous communities. For F>Fc communities overlap and feature overlap between neighbours falls toward ~1/q. Average degree is non-monotonic in F and clustering peaks at Fc.
key_points.evidence_quote: nodes are segregated into loosely-connected homogeneous communities in the former phase, while the majority of the communities overlap with each other in the latter phase

key_points.claim: The transition is set by the scaling variable N/q^F: it occurs when the number of matching nodes falls to the order of the typical WSN degree. Example: Fc=4 for q=5 gives 80 matching nodes, against a mean degree of 47.
key_points.evidence_quote: The transition occurs when $\tilde{N}$ becomes less than the typical degree for the original WSN model.

key_points.claim: Local attachment with link reinforcement amplifies homophily. Without LA, or with reinforcement disabled (wr=0), the transition disappears and results match a null model. Segregation therefore emerges without any trait-change (opinion-dynamics) mechanism.
key_points.evidence_quote: a key ingredient for the transition is the presence of LA rule

key_points.claim: Segregation slows information spreading. In SI simulations on networks with similar degree and link weights, spreading in the overlapping phase was about 2x faster than in the segregated phase.
key_points.evidence_quote: the spreading speed in the overlapping phase is approximately two times faster than for the segregated phase

key_points.claim: Simulation setup: N=50000 agents, pΔ=0.02, pr=0.001, pd=0.005, wr=1. Runs used 5×10^4 to 8×10^5 Monte Carlo steps to equilibrate. Communities were detected with multilevel Infomap, and the OACIS framework managed the parameter scans.

Implications and limits: if ties form on few features or few trait options, society segregates, which the authors link to echo chambers. Planned extensions are feature updates combined with triadic closure, heterogeneous q per feature, and individual differences in F. The authors contrast the model with Schelling-type models and with opinion-dynamics models.
key_points.evidence_quote: if the selection mechanism of acquaintances is based on very few features (F is small) and/or if traits a feature can take are limited only to few options (g is small), then the society will be segregated

reliability_notes: Full text was available. The paper is a peer-reviewed physics-style network model, not a general ABM or artificial-society survey. It is relevant to the social network formation, homophily, segregation and culture (Axelrod-like) aspects. Results are simulation-only, with no empirical validation. Some spreading results come from single runs.
